title: Government as an Operating System
summary: Constitutions are kernels: they define the system calls (powers), the permission model (rights), and the process isolation (separation of powers).
body:
Gov OS: the operating system of government — how public decisions are scheduled, how authority is permissioned, how services are delivered, and how the whole thing stays accountable. Civics as systems thinking.

Constitutions are kernels: they define the system calls (powers), the permission model (rights), and the process isolation (separation of powers). Everything else is user space — policy running on constitutional hardware.

title: Separation of Powers: Process Isolation
summary: Legislative, executive, judicial: three processes that can't corrupt each other's memory.
body:
Legislative, executive, judicial: three processes that can't corrupt each other's memory. Checks and balances are the IPC protocol — deliberate friction as a security feature.

title: Federalism: Distributed Systems
summary: Federalism is distributed computing: states are nodes with local state, the federation handles consensus.
body:
Federalism is distributed computing: states are nodes with local state, the federation handles consensus. CAP theorem applies: consistency, availability, partition tolerance — pick two, even in civics.

Public budgets are the ultimate scheduling problem: finite revenue, infinite demands. Appropriations are memory allocation; deficits are overcommit; audits are the garbage collector.

title: Emergency Powers: Kernel Panic Mode
summary: Emergencies switch the system to a privileged mode: faster decisions, fewer checks.
body:
Emergencies switch the system to a privileged mode: faster decisions, fewer checks. Like kernel panic handling, it must be bounded — sunset clauses return the system to normal.

title: Rights: The Immutable Permissions
summary: Constitutional rights are permissions even root can't revoke without the full amendment process.
body:
